Series::median¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::median() const -> Series
Series::median(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series

What It Does¶

median() finds the centre of an ordered population. For an odd number of values, that is the one middle value. For an even number, there are two middle values and the result is their arithmetic mean. It therefore returns float64 and may produce a number that did not occur in the source.

The no-argument overload uses every element as one population. The axis overload works independently along every lane of dim, then removes that axis from the result shape. NaN is not treated as missing: it propagates through a reduced population. Choose nanmedian() when omission is the intended data policy.

Overload Map¶

Call

Population

Result

x.median()

every value in x

scalar Series

x.median(dim)

each lane along dim

x.shape() without dim

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t) selects the axis to reduce. 0 is the outermost axis; -1 is the final axis. It must identify an existing axis. There is no keepdim overload, so the reduced dimension is always removed.

Returns¶

A new float64 Series. The source is unchanged. Global reduction has scalar shape []; axis reduction has one result for every remaining coordinate.

Gradient¶

Median is an order statistic. The identity of the selected middle observation can change abruptly when values cross or tie, so it is not a smooth reduction to use as a differentiable objective.

Examples¶

Example 1. An even population averages its two centre values.

auto values = pluss::make_series({4.0, 1.0, 3.0, 2.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, values.median());

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=2.5000

Ordering gives [1, 2, 3, 4]; the result is (2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5.

Example 2. dim=0 makes every column its own ordered population.

auto table = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 8.0, 3.0},
    {4.0, 2.0, 6.0},
    {7.0, 5.0, 9.0},
});
std::cout << table.median(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 5, 6]

The columns order to [1, 4, 7], [2, 5, 8], and [3, 6, 9].

Example 3. -1 reduces the final axis, here each row.

std::cout << table.median(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[3, 4, 7]

Example 4. Ordinary median preserves the presence of NaN.

auto missing = pluss::make_series({
    1.0, std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), 5.0, 9.0});
std::cout << missing.median();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=nan

Example 5. The NaN-skipping variant filters before ordering.

std::cout << missing.median() << "\n";
std::cout << missing.nanmedian();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=nan
pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=5

Example 6. Out-of-range axes are rejected rather than flattened.

try { std::cout << table.median(3); }
catch (const std::exception& error) { std::cout << error.what(); }

Output¶

quantile: dim out of range

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • This returns a value, not its source index.

  • NaN propagates; infinity remains an ordered endpoint.

  • The current axis diagnostic comes from the shared quantile kernel and says quantile: dim out of range.

Summary¶

Use median() for one robust centre or median(dim) for one per lane. It averages the two centres of even populations, removes the reduced axis, and preserves NaN rather than silently excluding it.
